How to read this document. Every terminal block is the verbatim output of the command shown above it, captured to a file at the moment it ran and reproduced here unedited. Every screenshot was taken from the deployed site with headless Chrome. The files are in the repository under submission/evidence/ and submission/screenshots/, so any claim here can be checked against its source.

1. Summary

The brief asked for four things: complete the Quickstart, complete the Walkthrough, report the bugs encountered, and — as a bonus — go beyond the first contract with an initial use case.

All four are done. The bonus is not a proposal on paper: it is a second TEE contract that ran on testnet and issued real receipts.

Fifteen findings are documented with reproduction steps. Five block a new developer outright. Five of the fifteen were only discoverable by running a contract against the live network, and those are the most useful material here:

  • T-12 — importing signing@2.1.0 stops the contract from instantiating. Registration succeeds, then every call returns an opaque HTTP 500 with an empty contract log, including calls to functions that never touch signing.
  • T-11 — tenant.claim() returns HTTP 500 on a tenant the SSO page already provisioned, rather than reporting already-admitted.
  • T-13 — contract ids are minted per registration and map ACLs bind to the id, so every re-register silently invalidates every ACL.
  • T-14 — kv-store.scan returns raw CAS pointer envelopes where kv-store.get resolves them, with no error from the host.
  • T-15 — the 20,000 credit grant was exhausted by ten registrations, against an advertised "~5,000 protected actions".

The use case, Nullstamp, issues verifiable consent receipts for agent calls that touch personal data. Its central claim — that anyone outside the node can recompute a receipt — is demonstrated in section 12 with a live receipt and an independent verifier, not asserted.

Two absences are deliberate and worth stating.

Plain http is not imported. Nullstamp has exactly one way out — http-with-placeholders — so no path inside this contract can send data without passing through host-side marker resolution. That is a design choice, not a default.

signing@2.1.0 is not imported either, but for a different reason: importing it prevents the contract from being instantiated at all. See finding T-12.

5. Quickstart — and the first two findings

The first code sample on the Quickstart page cannot run as written. Two causes, both forced by the SDK's own types: trustAnchor is required and T3nConfigError throws in the constructor before any network traffic, and the handshake needs the full handler set from createDefaultHandlers rather than EthSign alone. The same defective sample appears on the claim page, so it exists on two surfaces.

The corrected form works on the first attempt, and the DID the server returns matches the claim page character for character — which confirms the whole derivation path from API key to Ethereum address to DID:

This step reads tenant.me() first and skips the claim when the tenant is already active. That is not laziness — it is finding T-11. The SSO claim page has already created the tenant row and credited the account, and calling tenant.claim() against an active tenant answers:

RPC Error: Internal error [28113ed7-3a9d-45ef-98b8-b664fd9eb421]
RPC Error: Internal error [d8dbb69a-758f-4a4a-a67e-1e52b2f4b742]

Two attempts, two request ids, same result — while every read against the same tenant succeeds and reports status: active. The response shape implies the call is meant to be idempotent, so a setup script that trusts that gets blocked on a step that was already finished.

Step 4b exists because of finding T-13

Map ACLs bind to the numeric contract id, and every registration mints a new one. So any code change silently breaks every map the contract depends on. Across this exercise the same contract held ten ids: 615, 617, 618, 619, 620, 621, 638, 639, 641, 653 — neither contiguous nor predictable, so they cannot be pre-authorised. maps.update fixes it and appears in no documentation page.

8. The bug that cost the most time — T-12

Registration of version 0.1.0 succeeded and returned contract id 615. Then every call to it failed:

RPC Error: Internal error [754f19f6-b496-4f2d-b475-add668c7d85e]

Three properties made this hard to attribute:

  1. Registration succeeded — the rejection happens later, at instantiation.
  2. contracts.logs returned {"entries": []}. The contract never starts, so it cannot log anything about its own failure.
  3. list-receipts, which only scans a KV map and touches neither HTTP nor signing, failed identically.

So the signal pointed nowhere near the cause. I bisected by removing imported interfaces one at a time. The cause was host:interfaces/signing@2.1.0, declared in host-interfaces-2.1.0/package.wit at line 159 with nothing marking it unavailable to tenant contracts. Removing that single import — changing nothing else — turned the opaque 500 into a precise and genuinely excellent error:

access denied: TenantContract(did:t3n:f21dce…/617)
  cannot read map "z:f21dce…:receipts"

Suggested fix. Reject the registration when the world imports an interface the tenant runtime does not provide, and name the interface in the error. Either that, or mark availability per interface in host-interfaces.

Worth saying plainly: when the contract actually runs, the error messages are very good. That access-denied message names the principal, the id, the map, and the operation. The problem is concentrated in the cases where the contract never starts, where the message degrades to Internal error and the log is empty.

Several things here are load-bearing. response_code is 200, so the outbound call really left the enclave and reached the upstream. extracted shows the response was parsed, which is only possible if the round trip happened. seq_no and issued_at_secs come from the cluster, not from my machine.

And core lists only field names. The values are absent and cannot be present, because the code that assembles that section never receives them.

The log names the field count and never the field values. That is the discipline the whole design exists to enforce, and it holds even in the debugging surface.

Getting list-receipts to return parseable rows required finding T-14: kv-store.scan returns the raw CAS pointer envelope — ASCII magic T3VR followed by JSON holding a value_cid — where kv-store.get resolves it. The WIT promises key/value pairs and says nothing about this. The host raises no error; the bytes are simply the wrong bytes.

That receipt is what section 17 verifies, and the verification needs no
credits, no session, and no network. Which is precisely the point of the
design: the account is now at zero and the node will no longer answer us,
yet the receipt remains checkable by anyone, forever.

12. The central claim, demonstrated

A receipt that only its issuer can check is not a receipt. So the digest is computed over a canonical form: object keys ascending, no whitespace, array order preserved.

Here is the live receipt checked by a separate TypeScript program that imports no SDK, opens no session, and makes no network request — with the tenant account at zero credits:

Source: submission/evidence/17-verify-offline.txt

$ npm run verify:offline -- ../submission/live-receipt.json

receipt_id      : rcpt_8fb056c99bbea7e655d72075

17. All fifteen findings

Full text with verbatim quotes, suggested fixes, and reproduction steps for every finding is at docs/BUGS.md.

IDWeightSummary
T-01blockerFirst Quickstart sample cannot run: trustAnchor is required and throws in the constructor. Same defect on the claim page
T-02blockerQuickstart handler set incomplete for the handshake; createDefaultHandlers is never mentioned
T-03blockerDocs say tenant_did() is a string; WIT returns list<u8> and the reference repo hex-encodes it. Walkthrough sample does not compile
T-11blockertenant.claim() returns 500 on an already-provisioned tenant instead of already-admitted. Two request ids supplied
T-12blockerImporting signing@2.1.0 makes the contract fail to instantiate. Registration succeeds; every call then returns an opaque 500 with an empty contract log
T-13confusingContract ids are per registration and map ACLs bind to the id, so every re-register silently invalidates every ACL. Ten ids observed, non-contiguous
T-14confusingkv-store.scan returns raw T3VR CAS pointers where get resolves them; no error, not in the WIT
T-15confusing20,000 credit grant exhausted by ten registrations, against an advertised "~5,000 protected actions". One call locks 10,000,000,000 of a 20,000,000,000 grant
T-04confusingThe tenant claim step is not documented anywhere
T-05confusingmaps.create needs a contractId that only exists after registration, which the Walkthrough sequences later
T-06confusingSDK install reports 4 advisories, 1 critical (Zip Slip in decompress via jco)
T-07time sinkcontracts.logs, maps.entrySet, maps.entryGet, maps.getStatus, maps.update appear in no documentation page
T-08time sinkError-handling sample's catch-all arm collapses PlaceholderDenied and PlaceholderNoUserContext, whose distinction the WIT calls deliberate
T-09time sinkTwo doc URLs return 404; the payroll example page has no content
T-10time sinkReference repo version numbers disagree across world.wit, Cargo.toml, and a test name. The version lives in three places with no single source of truth — this bit me too
U-01proposalset-claims-digest deserves a documentation page of its own

18. One proposal

kv-store.set-claims-digest deserves a documentation page of its own.

Its WIT comment says the digest is planted in the transaction's Merkle leaf "so clients can verify receipts offline". That sentence answers the hardest question about confidential computing: how can anyone outside check work performed somewhere they cannot see? No ADK page discusses it.

This project is built on that capability, and the result holds up under an independent verifier — as section 12 shows, with the account at zero credits and the node no longer answering. Give it a page with a worked canonical-form example, and the pitch for T3N changes from "trust the enclave" to "compute it yourself and compare". That is a materially stronger claim, and the machinery already ships.

19. Reproducing all of this

git clone https://github.com/bryankwandou/nullstamp
cd nullstamp/contract/z-tenant-nullstamp
cargo test --target "$(rustc -vV | sed -n 's/^host: //p')"
cargo build --target wasm32-wasip2 --release
wasm-tools component wit target/wasm32-wasip2/release/z_tenant_nullstamp.wasm

cd ../../scripts
npm install
npm run preflight                    # no developer key needed

cp .env.example .env                 # set T3N_API_KEY
npm run step:01                      # through step:11
npm run verify:offline -- ../submission/live-receipt.json

The offline verification at the end needs no key, no credits, and no network, so it can be run by anyone from a clean clone.
